advances: This gives the general measure-level Helly-centerpoint theorem and, using the exact mixed-integer Helly number, the source-certified lower bound \(1/[2^n(d+1)]\).  It also checks that for mixed volume of a positive-mass convex body the selected mixed-integer point actually lies in that body.  The factor still depends on \(d\), so this is a baseline interface and does not prove the dimension-free locked target.
author: research-agent
external_sources:
Amitabh Basu and Timm Oertel, "Centerpoints: A Link between Optimization and Convex Geometry," SIAM Journal on Optimization 27(2) (2017), 866--889, DOI 10.1137/16M1092908; author manuscript: https://www.ams.jhu.edu/~abasu9/papers/centerpoints.pdf .  With \(F(S,\rho)\) defined as the maximum over \(x\in S\) of the minimum mass of a closed halfspace through and containing \(x\), their Theorem 15 states for a probability measure \(\rho\) supported on a nonempty closed \(S\) with finite \(h(S)\) that \(F(S,\rho)\ge1/h(S)\).  Their Corollary 16 specializes this to \(S=\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d\), giving \(1/[2^n(d+1)]\), in particular for mixed-volume measures of convex bodies.  Applying Theorem 15 to \(\rho=\mu/M\) and rescaling gives exactly the finite-measure statement proved above.  The proof above is self-contained and does not rely on the corrupted inequality signs in the local Markdown transcription.

Gennadiy Averkov and Robert Weismantel, "Transversal Numbers over Subsets of Linear Spaces," Advances in Geometry 12(1) (2012), 19--28, DOI 10.1515/advgeom.2011.028; primary preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/1002.0948 .  Theorem 1.1(3) states exactly \(h(\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb Z^q)=(r+1)2^q\) for nonnegative integers \(r,q\).  Taking \(r=d\), \(q=n\), and applying the coordinate permutation gives the Helly number used here.
proof:
We first prove the assertion for a general closed set \(S\).  Since the closed balls centered at the origin increase to \(\mathbb R^m\), continuity from below of the finite measure \(\mu\) gives a closed ball \(B\) such that
\[
\mu(B^c)<\frac{M}{h}.
\]
Consider the family of \(S\)-convex sets
\[
\mathcal F:=\{B\cap S\}\mathbin\cup
\{H\cap S:H\text{ is a closed halfspace and }\mu(H)>M-M/h\}.
\]

Every subfamily of \(\mathcal F\) having at most \(h\) members has nonempty intersection.  Indeed, take \(r\) halfspace members \(H_1\cap S,\ldots,H_r\cap S\), and let \(\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}\) record whether \(B\cap S\) is also present.  If \(r+\varepsilon\le h\), then, using \(\mu(S^c)=0\),
\[
\mu\!\left(S^c\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^r H_i^c\cup
  \begin{cases}B^c,&\varepsilon=1,\\ \varnothing,&\varepsilon=0,
  \end{cases}\right)
<\frac{(r+\varepsilon)M}{h}\le M.
\]
Here \(\mu(H_i^c)=M-\mu(H_i)<M/h\), and the same strict bound holds for \(B^c\).  Thus the complement of the chosen intersection has measure strictly less than \(M\); the intersection has positive measure and is therefore nonempty.  This includes \(h=1\), as well as subfamilies with fewer than \(h\) members.

It follows that \(\mathcal F\) has the finite-intersection property.  For a finite subfamily with at least \(h\) members, every \(h\) members intersect by the preceding paragraph, so the defining \(S\)-Helly property gives intersection of the whole finite subfamily; for fewer than \(h\) members the preceding paragraph applies directly.  Moreover, every member is closed and \(B\cap S\) is compact.  Equivalently, intersect every member of \(\mathcal F\) with the compact set \(B\cap S\); these are closed subsets of \(B\cap S\) with the finite-intersection property.  Compactness therefore gives
\[
\bigcap_{F\in\mathcal F}F\ne\varnothing.
\]
Fix \(x\) in this intersection.  In particular, \(x\in S\), and \(x\) belongs to every closed halfspace of measure strictly greater than \(M-M/h\).

Let \(G\) be any closed halfspace containing \(x\).  The whole-space case is immediate.  Otherwise write
\[
G=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:a\cdot y\le b\}
\]
with \(a\ne0\).  Suppose for contradiction that \(\mu(G)<M/h\).  For \(j\ge1\), set
\[
H_j:=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:a\cdot y\ge b+1/j\}.
\]
The closed halfspaces \(H_j\) increase to the open complement \(G^c=\{a\cdot y>b\}\).  Hence continuity from below gives
\[
\mu(H_j)\uparrow\mu(G^c)=M-\mu(G)>M-M/h.
\]
For some \(j\), therefore, \(\mu(H_j)>M-M/h\).  The definition of \(x\) forces \(x\in H_j\), whereas \(x\in G\) and \(G\cap H_j=\varnothing\), a contradiction.  Thus \(\mu(G)\ge M/h\).  Notice that this argument neither excludes atoms nor assumes that hyperplanes have zero mass: the boundary of \(G\) remains inside \(G\), while the increasing union of the \(H_j\) is exactly its open complement.

We now specialize.  Averkov and Weismantel's mixed-integer Helly theorem gives, for all \(r,q\ge0\),
\[
h(\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb Z^q)=(r+1)2^q.
\]
The coordinate permutation between \(\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb Z^n\) and \(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d\) is an invertible linear map; it carries convex sets to convex sets and preserves all intersection statements.  Therefore
\[
h(\Lambda)=h(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)=2^n(d+1).
\]
Applying the first part with \(S=\Lambda\) proves the asserted bound for every nonzero finite Borel measure supported on \(\Lambda\).

Finally, for a convex body \(C\), compactness of its projection onto \(\mathbb R^n\) implies that only finitely many lattice vectors \(z\) can index nonempty fibers.  Thus \(\mu_C\) is a finite Borel measure, and by construction it is supported on \(C\cap\Lambda\), hence also on \(\Lambda\).  When \(W>0\), the preceding conclusion supplies \(x\in\Lambda\) having the stated positive depth.  If \(x\notin C\), strict separation of the point \(x\) from the compact convex set \(C\) gives \(a\ne0\) such that
\[
a\cdot x>\sup_{y\in C}a\cdot y.
\]
Then the closed halfspace \(G:=\{y:a\cdot y\ge a\cdot x\}\) contains \(x\) and is disjoint from \(C\), so \(\mu_C(G)=0\).  This contradicts \(\mu_C(G)\ge W/[2^n(d+1)]>0\).  Hence \(x\in C\cap\Lambda\), completing the proof.
statement:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty and closed.  Define its \(S\)-Helly number \(h(S)\) to be the least positive integer \(h\) such that the following holds: for every finite family of sets of the form \(S\cap K_i\), with each \(K_i\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) convex, if every \(h\) members have nonempty intersection, then all members have nonempty intersection.  Suppose \(h:=h(S)<\infty\), and let \(\mu\) be a nonzero finite Borel measure on \(\mathbb R^m\) satisfying \(\mu(\mathbb R^m\setminus S)=0\).  Put \(M:=\mu(\mathbb R^m)>0\).  Then there exists \(x\in S\) such that every closed halfspace \(G\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) containing \(x\) satisfies
\[
\mu(G)\ge \frac{M}{h(S)}.
\]

Consequently, for all integers \(n,d\ge0\), every nonzero finite Borel measure \(\nu\) supported on
\[
\Lambda:=\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d
\]
has a point \(x\in\Lambda\) such that every closed halfspace \(G\ni x\) satisfies
\[
\nu(G)\ge \frac{\nu(\mathbb R^{n+d})}{2^n(d+1)}.
\]

In particular, let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+d}\) be a convex body and let its mixed-volume measure be
\[
\mu_C(A):=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\mathcal H_d\bigl(\{y\in\mathbb R^d:(z,y)\in A\cap C\}\bigr)
\]
for Borel \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+d}\).  If \(W:=\mu_C(\mathbb R^{n+d})>0\), then the point can be chosen in \(C\cap\Lambda\), and every closed halfspace \(G\ni x\) satisfies \(\mu_C(G)\ge W/[2^n(d+1)]\).
